(01:02:13): And when you're trying to be super cautious of your resources, you have to ignore some of that because then you're able to roll out things once, which is important, but in addition to that, every new A/B test you want to run or every new hypothesis you have, if you now have a version of your app that's different in Mexico, in China, in India, whatever, you're going to have to run that test and whatever change you have in all of those versions, and then you just start having all of these different versions of the app everywhere and good luck managing that in terms of code, in terms of processes, in terms of personnel, in terms of costs, and most importantly in terms of time because now every single experiment or hypothesis is going to take you way longer to be able to deploy, and time is almost more important than money when you're a startup. So, it's important to keep things super simple, and this was something that we did that actually ended up paying off with few exceptions like India and China.
turns.zh:
我认为这非常具有争议性，因为当你在受监管的行业工作时，尤其是在B2B场景下，关注特定国家的情况至关重要。研究特定国家及其文化元素很重要，特别是当你需要处理法律差异等问题时。国家之间的差异确实存在，但人类本质上是相似的。我们自认为差异巨大，但其实只是成长环境不同。例如，在巴西人们喜欢跳舞，在墨西哥人们跳萨尔萨舞，有些地方允许拥抱，而有些地方则不然。诚然，文化差异确实存在，我们应当接纳多样性并适应不同文化，但涉及人类核心行为的这些差异，往往是理解他人的最后5%关键所在。

（01:00:27）对于初创公司而言，无论处于早期阶段与否，若过度关注群体间的细微差异，往往会犯下严重错误——过早实施大量变更、学习效率低下、代码复杂度与组织架构复杂度急剧攀升。以Duolingo为例，作为面向消费者的应用，我们无需应对太多监管问题，除中国需注意某些词汇限制外，用户普遍希望以特定方式学习语言、使用应用。因此存在诸多共通之处。我们曾以"全球统一标准"为指导原则：若某项A/B测试在某地奏效，便会认为其适用于所有市场。但每当我将Duolingo推向新市场时，总会遭遇类似反馈——"这里情况不同，人群差异巨大，
就时间而言，如今每项实验或假设的实施都需要耗费大量时间，而对于初创公司而言，时间几乎比金钱更为重要。因此，保持事务的极度简洁至关重要。除印度和中国等少数例外情况外，我们采取的这一策略最终确实带来了回报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such cool advice. It reminds me of a quote that I think of that a friend of mine shared once, "Life is maintenance. Anything you add to your life is just something you're going to have to maintain from that point forward," and similar in products. Any time you add new code, you're going to maintain that code forever, and the more you can not add anything new and not make things really different, the easier everything gets. People forget that. It's like, "Oh, we're just going to spend a bunch of time to make it awesome in China or Brazil," and then, oh, they have to maintain that forever and every you feature has to...
turns.zh: 真是个超棒的建议。这让我想起我一位朋友曾分享过的一句话：“生活就是维护。任何你添加到生活中的东西，从那时起你就必须一直维护它。” 在产品开发中也是如此。每当你添加新代码，就意味着要永远维护这段代码。若能避免添加新功能、避免让产品产生重大变动，一切都会变得简单许多。人们却常常忽视这一点——比如他们会说：“哦，我们只需花些时间让产品在中国或巴西变得超棒。” 但随后却发现，维护这些功能永无止境，每个新功能都必须……

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: And it's an 80/20, so just focus on what will get you the 80 and not the 20. And then when you have the luxury of focusing on the 20, then you can.
turns.zh: 这就是二八法则，所以要专注于能为你带来80%收益的部分，而非20%的那部分。等你有余力关注那20%时，再去处理也不迟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, speaking of different cultures and people being different but not that different, you pivoted your career basically to focus on Latin America. First of all, why did you decide to do that? That's a pretty unique path and what pulled you there?
turns.zh: 说到不同文化和人虽然不同但又不算太不同，你转行专注于拉丁美洲市场。首先，你为什么会做出这样的选择？这条职业道路相当独特，是什么因素促使你转向这个方向的？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: So Lenny, I don't see it as a pivot because as we were joking in the beginning, I've been an employee, I was an operator there at early stage startups and now I'm a founder and I'm a VC, so I'm still kind of in this little stack of roles that we have in our little tech ecosystem. And in my time working with Tumblr and my agency and Duolingo, I had the pleasure of speaking with entrepreneurs all over the world, in part because I started getting some media because of the work that I've been doing starting at Tumblr, so a lot of entrepreneurs reached out to me, but also because I became a mentor for an organization called Endeavor, which is global. So, I started working with entrepreneurs in Japan and Brazil on my free time, just mentoring. And I know that the opportunity for growth in terms of tech in Latin America is huge because first of all, the opportunity for growth in tech is huge all over the world, meaning there's just more and more to do. (01:05:09): There's more pieces of our lives that can become more efficient or better or cheaper by making them digital in some way, shape or form because digital products scale. We are behind when it comes to that in terms of Latin America, and our economy is also not doing super great right now. There's a number of things that make it tougher to succeed in Latin America, but make the outcome of potential success much higher. And simply put, there's a lot of low hanging fruit because a lot of what has already been digitized and productized in the US and more developed markets just hasn't in Latin America. And every time I took these calls, I would think like, "Well, this is not very efficient for me to be doing this one-to-one call. I feel very good about myself, I feel great, and this entrepreneur learned a lot, but I wish I could do this more at scale." (01:05:56): And also it doesn't seem like this is what's going to help this entrepreneur succeed. Maybe it's a little bit of advice, but it's like... And not only that, but I had a lot of experiences where I would mention something about growth that I had learned and that would blow the entrepreneur's mind. And I would think, "Why do I know this, but not this entrepreneur who honestly is smarter and more ambitious than me?" Oh, it's because I've had a career in Silicon Valley. It's because I've gotten to work with some of the best people in the world and I have access to this information just free flowing in my way all the time, and we take it for granted. So, how can we make this more accessible to Latin America's entrepreneurs, so that they can have access to that? What else is hard to get access to that could really get in the way? (01:06:34): Oh, like access to capital. So, what's the VC in the angel ecosystem looking like and what can we do that can actually impact that at scale? And then there's other pieces of the ecosystem that are missing, like if you're going to start a company, you have to incorporate it. It sounds super boring, but Brazil is one of the countries that takes the longest time to incorporate a company in the world, but then if you're going to get investment, you probably can't get investment in your Brazil entity because investors are like, "I don't know anything about Brazil, and sounds like a lot of employers get sued by their employees and lose," which is totally true, "And there's all this liability. I feel much more comfortable investing in a Delaware company." So then entrepreneurs are like, "Oh man, now I have to create this entity in Delaware. I don't even know where that is and what's the C-core? What's this other thing?" (01:07:19): So, there's just stuff that needs to happen for Latin Americans that we don't think about here, "Silicon Valley" talking about it as in the cloud in the US and developed markets, but also then you're able to raise money, how do you get money down to your country? That's not simple at all. How do you think about the FX transactions and not get screwed in the process and who's going to do it? And so anyway, there's a number of these things that make it super hard. And so, that's some of the problems that we wanted to solve. (01:07:47): Why it matters to me? I'm Brazilian, I'm Latin American, and I know that I had all of the opportunities in the world. I went to an American school, I got to go to school in the US, I got to work with some of the best tech companies in the world, and 99.9% of people in Latin America will not have these opportunities. And so for me, if I don't use this privilege to somehow make a huge impact where I came from, that will last, then I kind of wasted my life. So, that's why this matters so much to me, and I met my co-founder, Brian Requarth at On Deck. If you've heard of On Deck before, I'm a big fan.
turns.zh:
伦尼，我不认为这算得上是职业转型，因为正如我们开场时开玩笑说的，我曾在早期初创公司担任员工、运营人员，如今又成为创始人和风险投资人，始终在科技生态圈的不同角色中切换。在与Tumblr、我的代理公司以及Duolingo合作期间，我有幸与世界各地的创业者交流，部分原因是我在Tumblr的工作逐渐获得了媒体关注，许多创业者主动联系我；另一方面，我还成为全球性组织Endeavor的导师，开始在业余时间为日本和巴西的创业者提供指导。

我深知拉丁美洲科技领域的增长潜力巨大。首先，全球科技行业的增长机遇无处不在，意味着待开发的领域越来越多。（01:05:09）：通过某种形式将生活数字化，我们能显著提升效率、优化体验、降低成本，因为数字产品具有规模化优势。在拉丁美洲，我们在这方面落后于发达市场，且当前经济形势也不乐观。诸多因素制约着当地创业成功，但潜在成功的可能性也更高——许多美国及发达市场已实现数字化和产品化的领域在拉美尚未普及。每次接听电话时，我都会想：“一对一沟通效率太低。虽然我自我感觉良好、收获满满，但希望能更大规模地提供帮助。”（01:05:56）

此外，现有建议似乎难以助力创业者成功。或许有些建议有用，但更多时候……我曾多次提及已掌握的增长策略，却让创业者惊叹不已。我不禁反思：“为何我知晓这些，而这位比我更聪明、更有雄心的创业者却未曾听闻？”答案在于我在硅谷的职业生涯——接触过全球顶尖人才，信息触手可及却被视为理所当然。如何让拉美创业者也能享有这些资源？还有哪些难以获取的资源阻碍着他们？（01:06:34）

比如获取资本的渠道。在天使投资生态中，VC与初创企业的合作模式如何？如何通过规模化行动真正影响这一体系？生态链中还有哪些缺失环节？例如，公司注册流程繁琐。巴西是全球公司注册耗时最长的国家之一，而巴西实体难以获得投资，因为投资者担忧当地劳动纠纷风险。这时，德拉瓦州公司就成了更优选择。创业者不得不为此耗费精力——他们甚至不清楚德拉瓦州的法律体系和公司治理框架。
还有其他事情吗？（01:07:19）：所以，对于拉丁美洲人来说，有很多事情是我们在这里想不到的。比如，硅谷谈论的云计算服务在美国和发达市场可能很常见，但在拉丁美洲，要想融资却并非易事。你要如何把资金引入本国？这绝非易事。如何处理外汇交易，避免被坑，又该由谁来负责这些事务？总之，诸多复杂问题让这件事变得异常艰难。这正是我们想要解决的难题之一。（01:07:47）：为什么这对我如此重要？我是巴西人，来自拉丁美洲。我深知自己曾拥有无数机遇。我曾就读于美国学校，有机会在美国求学，还能与全球顶尖科技公司合作。但拉丁美洲99.9%的人都无法获得这些机会。对我而言，如果不利用这些特权为家乡带来持久的影响，那简直就是虚度光阴。所以这件事对我意义非凡。我和联合创始人布莱恩·雷夸斯（Brian Requarth）是在On Deck认识的。如果你们听说过On Deck，我可是它的忠实粉丝。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm wearing On Deck socks right now. Yeah, I am.
turns.zh: 我现在正穿着On Deck的袜子。是的，我现在就穿着。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: I love their socks, and I just had a conversation with them yesterday. I am a big fan of what they built. I met Brian doing On Deck... I actually was thinking of starting a completely different company, but also focused on community. As we were talking about, people want to find connection, and I think that there's a lot of business opportunity there, but I met my co-founder and he was working with our third co-founder, Yuri, who was actually the guy... We joke he's the guy who builds things. (01:08:53): He's the CTO, he actually knows how to build and started talking about what it is that we can do to make an impact in the speed at which tech startups succeed in Latin America because we think we can have a huge impact on the GDP of the whole region, developments, job opportunities, and so on and so forth. So to me, that's what motivates me. It's like figuring out how I can use my time as leverage to make the biggest impact possible in terms of socioeconomical mobility for people in the world and focusing on the part of the world that I came from made the most sense.
turns.zh: 我超爱他们的袜子，昨天我还和他们聊过天。我特别欣赏他们打造的这个平台。我认识布莱恩是在On Deck……其实我原本打算创办一家完全不同的公司，但也致力于社区事业。我们聊天时发现，大家都渴望建立人际联系，我觉得这蕴藏着巨大的商业机遇。不过后来我遇到了我的联合创始人，他当时正和我们的第三位联合创始人尤里合作。尤里是那种……我们开玩笑说他是动手能力超强的人。（01:08:53）他是首席技术官，深谙技术开发之道。我们开始探讨如何加速拉丁美洲科技初创企业的成功进程，因为我们相信这能对整个地区的GDP增长、经济发展和就业机会创造产生巨大影响。对我而言，这就是我的动力所在。关键在于如何利用自己的时间创造最大价值，助力全球人民实现社会经济流动性，而选择聚焦我出生的这片土地，就显得格外顺理成章。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you referenced this company, that you started Latitud. Maybe just describe briefly, just broadly, how do you pitch what Latitud does to folks that might find it useful?
turns.zh: 你之前提到了你创立的Latitud公司。能不能简单介绍一下，让听众了解它的核心价值？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: I will, and I still do a pretty bad job with pitching it, but the pitch is basically we're building the operating system for Latin American early stage tech startups, and what that means is that building a startup is hard anywhere, but it's extra hard in Latin America for some of the reasons that I outlined. Some of the things that we decided to solve for are one, it's super lonely to be a founder. And if you're able to meet great founders who are just a step ahead of you in anything, be it in product or growth or marketing or incorporation or finances, you can save yourself so much time from trying to read books and Google if they can just tell you what to do or connect you with the right person, that if we were able to connect these people meaningfully, we could make a huge impact. (01:10:16): So, that's number one, it's lonely. And number two, you build a startup in Brazil and you're like, "Wow, this is working. I'm going to go to Silicon Valley." I've seen this happen a lot in the past decade, and Silicon Valley is a completely different place. The US, it's a different place, the competition's different. 3% of people in Brazil only, and that varies in Latin America, speak English. So, the likelihood of you being taken seriously is low. Your chances of success are low, but at the same time, Latin America has so much in common as a region, but we don't actually actually see that if we're Latin Americans. We just think we're countries, especially Brazilians don't think that they're part of the rest, and Mexicans don't think about Brazil. It's so far, look at it on the map. In the US you're like, oh Latin America." (01:10:58): But if you're there, it's just not at all connected, but the opportunities of growth are huge and dependent on whether you meet the right people are able to open doors and understand that our problems are so similar that a solution for one part of this region could potentially be great for another part of the region. I'm not doing a great job of pitching, but in addition to it being lonely and it being difficult to find the right resources and really trustworthy knowledge, it's really hard to raise capital and it's really hard to do things like incorporate and bring your money down, et cetera. So, that's what we do. First, we have a fellowship program. We have 1,500 entrepreneurs who got in, we run four cohorts a year, about 600 applicants per, and so you get in and you get access to all of these resources we've put together. (01:11:44): You get to find out what everyone thinks about other investors in the region because I think it's important to disseminate that information. You get access to introductions to investors through each other and advice and events. In addition, we have a fund, so we've invested in 100 startups and we're raising our second fund now. It's going to be around $25 million with a $30 million cap, so that's another thing. So we invest, you figure out your investment game, but you might become one of our investments as well. And in addition, we have products that make it a lot easier to navigate the super, in my opinion, boring and frustrating stuff behind starting a company that you don't want to think about it as an entrepreneur because you're trying to solve a problem and build a team and build a product. (01:12:25): You're not trying to figure out what's the best incorporation method and how to open a bank account in the US and how to figure out the foreign exchange prices and bring the money down and how to manage that money or how to stay compliant in your country, and then in two other jurisdictions, if you have a Delaware and a Cayman. So, we do all of that for you and make it easy through a dashboard we built, a bank that we built, and so on and so forth. So, it's not an easy to describe business because it's kind of an ecosystem play. We're trying to elevate the tech ecosystem in Latin America, and it's a lot of moving parts.
turns.zh:
我会，而且我现在做得还是很糟糕，但核心要点是，我们正在为拉丁美洲早期科技初创企业打造操作系统。具体来说，创业在任何地方都不容易，但在拉丁美洲尤其困难，原因我在前面已经讲过。我们致力于解决的核心问题包括：首先，创始人往往感到孤立无援。如果能遇到比你领先一步的优秀创始人——无论是在产品、增长、营销、注册公司还是融资方面——他们能节省你大量时间，不必再去查书或谷歌搜索。只要能有效对接这些资源，我们就能产生巨大影响。（01:10:16）：第一，孤立感强烈。第二，你在巴西创办公司后，可能会想“哇，业务进展顺利，我要去硅谷了”。过去十年我见过太多这种情况，但硅谷与美国完全不同，竞争环境天差地别。拉丁美洲只有3%的人（各国比例不一）会说英语，所以被认真对待的可能性微乎其微。成功概率低，但另一方面，拉丁美洲作为一个地区其实有很多共性，但我们自己却没有意识到。我们只把彼此视为独立国家，尤其是巴西人不认为自己是拉美大家庭的一部分，墨西哥人也对巴西心存隔阂。看看地图就知道，美国人对拉丁美洲的认知仅停留在表面。而身处拉美的人却深感割裂，但这里蕴藏着巨大的发展机遇，前提是能结识对的人、打开局面，并意识到我们的问题本质上相通。比如，某个地区的解决方案可能惠及其他地区。我虽然不擅长推销，但除了孤立感、资源匮乏和融资难题外，注册公司、汇款等繁琐事务也令人头疼。我们的解决方案包括：第一，创业者赋能计划。我们有1500名参与者，分四期每年600人，成功入选者可获取整合资源的机会。（01:11:44）：他们能了解区域内其他投资者的动态——信息共享至关重要。还能通过彼此介绍获得投资机会、获取建议和参与活动。此外，我们还设立基金，已投资100家初创企业，目前筹备第二支基金，规模约2500万美元，目标3000万美元。投资后，我们会帮助创业者优化投资策略，甚至可能成为我们的投资对象。同时，我们开发产品，简化创业者不愿深究的繁琐事务，比如注册公司、美金账户开设、外汇兑换、资金管理和本地合规等。
其他司法管辖区，如果你同时拥有特拉华州和开曼群岛的公司架构。为此，我们通过自建的仪表板、搭建的银行平台等全方位为您提供便利。需要说明的是，这项业务的核心在于构建一个完整的生态系统。我们致力于提升拉丁美洲的科技生态系统水平，而这背后涉及诸多复杂的要素和环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You basically help them do everything, which is what I'm hearing, and it sounds like you'd be a fool not to take advantage of this. The customers essentially are founders in any Latin America country, is that right?
turns.zh: 基本上，你需要帮他们处理所有事务——这就是我听说的情况。听起来你要是错过这个机会就太傻了。我猜在拉丁美洲，客户本质上都是创业者，对吧？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: Founders in Latin America, but we also have a lot of US-based founders who are building for Latin America because they understand that the opportunity there is huge.
turns.zh: 是拉丁美洲的创业者，但我们也有很多总部位于美国的创业者，他们为拉丁美洲市场开发产品，因为他们深知那里的机遇巨大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, and then what is the arrangement? Do you take equity if they join the program? Is it free?
turns.zh: 太棒了，那具体的合作模式是怎样的？如果他们加入这个项目，你们会拿走股权吗？项目是免费加入的吗？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: We don't, joining the program is free. You just have to be able to get in. For a number of reasons, we just don't want to deter anyone who's amazing from being part of this community, and so that's why we made that decision. If we invest, we take equity. If you choose to use our products, that's a paid thing. So, you can choose what makes sense for you.
turns.zh: 我们不会收取股权。加入项目是免费的，但你得符合入选条件。出于多种原因，我们不想阻止任何优秀人才加入这个社区，所以我们做出了这样的决定。如果我们投资某个项目，就会持有股权。但如果你选择使用我们的产品，那就是付费服务了。所以，你可以根据自身情况选择最合适的方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I wanted to ask about is what is it that Latin American founders and companies are uniquely good at? Is there kind of a thread across Latin American startups that are like, oh, they're so good at this area, pay attention here?
turns.zh: 我想问的是，拉丁美洲的创业者和公司在哪些方面特别擅长？有没有贯穿整个拉丁美洲初创企业的共性，比如，他们在某个领域特别出色，值得关注？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: In general terms, startup founders have to be really scrappy and resourceful and resilient. Latin Americans tend to be very scrappy, resourceful, and resilient because of just the realities in which we were brought up in. We have words for that that we don't have in English and Portuguese in Spanish, which is like dancing around things and figuring out things when you don't have other solutions. So, I think that's something that we see a lot. In terms of what we're really good at, I would say first of all, there's opportunity in every single vertical in Latin America because it's such a wide open field, so there's opportunity everywhere. (01:14:40): It's not that we're particularly good at FinTech, for example, but if you look at the FinTech opportunity in Latin America right now, it's so hot and there's so much money and there's so much happening because of the huge problem of people not having access to bank accounts or access to credit, or just all of the bureaucracy that exists in trying to get those things or to make payments and so on and so forth. So, there's just huge opportunity there. I'm trying to think what else-
turns.zh: 总的来说，创业者必须非常灵活、善于资源整合且富有韧性。拉丁美洲人往往非常善于灵活应变、善于整合资源且富有韧性，这源于我们成长的环境所造就的特质。我们有一些在英语和西班牙语中找不到的词汇来形容这种特质，比如“舞龙”、“曲折前行”——即在没有其他解决方案时，通过灵活变通和创新来解决问题。所以我认为这在拉丁美洲很常见。说到我们擅长什么，我觉得首先，拉丁美洲每个垂直领域都存在巨大机遇，因为这片市场太广阔了，所以到处都有机会。（01:14:40）：比如，我们并非特别擅长金融科技，但看看拉丁美洲金融科技领域的机遇吧，当下非常火热，资金充足，发展迅速。这是因为人们无法获得银行账户、无法获得信贷，或者在获取这些服务时面临繁琐的官僚程序等问题。所以这里有巨大的机遇。我在想还有什么别的——

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: So there's just huge opportunity there. Trying to think what else I would highlight. Ah, Lenny, you talked about B2C. I think again, because there's so much open field, there's so much opportunity when it comes to B2B, especially when you're talking about SMBs. There's a lot of small and medium businesses doing things on paper, so figure out what they are and how you can make them not on paper and deploy them effectively. So I think that's an advantage we have. (01:15:28): Other than that, I wouldn't highlight anything in particular. I think that there's amazing people all over the world. It's just a matter of what are the opportunities that exist. And because there's so many opportunities that are Latin America specific or that are emerging market specific, which means that if they work in an emerging market in Latin America, they could work in other emerging markets. And you know what? Most of the world is not developed markets and understanding what it's like to not have access to amazing wifi and iPhones and all the things that we have access to, that can be a huge advantage because that's the reality that most of the population lives in. And that's a huge TAM.
turns.zh: 因此，那里存在着巨大的机遇。我再想想还有什么值得强调的。啊，Lenny，你提到了B2C业务。我认为同样，鉴于市场尚未完全开发，B2B领域存在着大量机遇，特别是针对中小企业而言。许多中小企业仍在使用纸质文件开展业务，因此需要了解他们的痛点，并找到让他们摆脱纸质流程、有效部署数字化工具的解决方案。我认为这正是我们的优势所在。（01:15:28）：除此之外，我没有特别要强调的方面。我认为全球各地都有杰出人才，关键在于如何把握现有的机遇。由于许多机遇专属于拉丁美洲或新兴市场，这意味着如果一项技术能在拉丁美洲的新兴市场成功应用，就很可能在其他新兴市场同样奏效。要知道，全球大部分地区并非发达市场。了解在缺乏高速无线网络和iPhone等先进设备的环境下如何开展业务，这本身就是一项巨大优势，因为这正是全球多数人口的现实生活场景。而这也构成了巨大的潜在市场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes me think about WhatsApp. And one of the reasons they made it is they were just obsessed with making the app incredibly small and fast. And they started, I think with international markets and then that just ended up being an amazing app so fast and so easy to use.
turns.zh: 这让我想到了WhatsApp。他们开发这款应用的初衷之一，就是执着于将应用做得极致轻便高效。我记得他们最初专注于国际市场，最终打造出了一款快速易用的惊艳应用。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: And still, and now there's things being built on top of WhatsApp. We just invested in a company called Leadsales, and they basically turn your WhatsApp into a CRM, which is amazing because so much business is being done on WhatsApp, and that's not the case here in the US. So you want to understand that you can build something for that. And there are other markets that are using WhatsApp for which that's also going to be useful. And the other thing is I think that emerging or developing markets tend to sometimes skip over things because we're so behind. (01:16:48): So for example, there's examples of these in India and in some countries in Africa where, I don't know, the desktop was skipped, people just went straight to mobile. I think we can see these catapult opportunities because then when you start building something and you didn't even build for the previous version of whatever it is that was being used because in the US or more developed market, you had access to them, then you are in a way at an advantage. So I'm excited to see how that plays out in the next few years, and I'm particularly curious to see how that plays out when it comes to AI.
turns.zh: 如今，基于WhatsApp的应用也在不断涌现。我们刚刚投资了一家名为Leadsales的公司，他们能将WhatsApp转变为CRM系统，这真是令人惊叹，因为大量业务都在WhatsApp上完成，而美国的情况并非如此。因此，你需要意识到可以为此开发产品。其他市场也正在利用WhatsApp，这同样具有实用价值。另外，我认为新兴或发展中市场有时会跳过某些阶段，因为我们起步较晚。（01:16:48）：例如，印度和非洲部分国家就存在这样的案例，比如桌面端直接跳到移动端。我认为我们能从中看到一些飞跃式机遇。当你开始开发某项产品时，若未针对美国或发达市场已有的版本进行优化，那么在某种程度上你就占据了先机。我很期待未来几年的发展，也特别好奇AI领域的机遇会如何演变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One last question around Latin America. It's going to be a broad question. What do you think people should be paying attention to, whether it's specific companies you want to call out, big companies that are doing great or just trends or patterns, what do you think people should be paying attention to? Anything you want to shout out?
turns.zh: 最后一个关于拉丁美洲的问题。这将是一个宽泛的提问。你认为人们应该关注哪些方面？无论是具体的公司、表现出色的巨头，还是趋势或模式，你认为人们应该关注什么？有没有什么值得大力推荐的？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: Lenny, the truth is I would love to call out all of our portfolio companies. I believe in all of them, and there are some of them that are growing incredibly impressively. One of them is Pomelo, which is a FinTech platform for FinTechs that is just grown incredibly. To me, it's more about paying attention to Latin America. I think for the US, that's already a lot. I don't think people know what's going on below the border, I have no idea what Brazil is like, but paying attention because it's not just a place that's behind and trying to catch up. It's a place where the opportunity to make a lot of money exists. It's a higher risk region because of all the political and economic instability. But given the scenario that we're in right now, which is that we're still behind in terms of all the solutions that we know will be built to give people access to health, to education, to financial services, et cetera. (01:18:36): But we actually have a lot of money flowing into the region in terms of venture capital. We have the best talent we've ever had because now we've had, I forget how many, but a lot of IPOs that came from Latin America and unicorn companies, people who have worked at those companies or who have worked places like Duolingo are coming back to build now, know what they're doing. And so there's a number of things that have come together that make now a really exciting time to build a startup in Latin America and to scale it. So from an investment perspective, I just think that there's a lot of hot opportunities now in terms of knowing what's a good opportunity versus not. I think the same rules probably apply to those anywhere else, which is most importantly, the entrepreneur. Does this person know what they're talking about? (01:19:23): Do they have an unfair advantage in terms of knowing what a problem that exists and knowing how to solve it in a way that others couldn't do? They have access to the best talent in the world, not just in the region that will actually join them and build the best thing possible. And yeah, what's the TAM? And not just what they put on the slide, but what you actually believe the TAM to be. So that's what I would say. I think everyone's looking at FinTech and Latin America right now. It's hot, it's profitable. Money is where the money is, but I'm super excited about what happens with health and education in particular because I think that that has the power to truly transform the region in a massive way. (01:20:05): At Latitud, I think I mentioned in addition to FinTech, we tend to invest a lot in B2B SMB platforms that are helping businesses scale and work more effectively because there is a huge need for that and there's an opportunity to build. And I think that that can have an impact on the region. So I think that would be my advice. It's a little broad, but other than that, if not, I would just now sit here and tell you 15 companies that we love at Latitud and I won't.
turns.zh: 莱尼，事实上我很想把我们所有的投资组合公司都介绍一遍。我对它们都充满信心，其中有些公司的发展速度令人惊叹。比如Pomelo，这是一个专为金融科技公司服务的平台，发展得极为迅速。对我来说，重点在于关注拉丁美洲市场。我认为对美国市场而言，关注拉美已经足够了。我觉得人们对拉美以南地区的情况知之甚少，比如巴西的情况我也知之甚少。但我们需要关注拉美，因为它不只是一个落后并努力追赶的地区，更是一个蕴藏着巨大商机的区域。尽管政治和经济不稳定，但鉴于我们目前所处的环境——在健康、教育、金融服务等领域的解决方案建设仍落后——（01:18:36）但实际上，大量风险投资正涌入该地区。我们拥有史上最优秀的人才储备，因为已有大量来自拉美地区的IPO公司和独角兽企业诞生。这些公司前员工或曾就职于Duolingo等平台的人才正回归创业，他们深谙行业之道。种种因素叠加，使得当下在拉美创办和发展初创企业成为极具吸引力的时机。从投资角度看，当前判断优质机会的标准与其他地区无异，最关键的是创业者是否专业——他们是否真正懂行？（01:19:23）他们是否在识别问题和解决方案方面具有独特优势？他们能否吸引全球顶尖人才？这些都是关键要素。至于TAM（目标市场规模），不仅要看PPT上的数据，更要基于真实认知。总之，我认为当下所有人都聚焦于金融科技和拉美市场。这里热度高、回报快，资金流向之处即商机所在。但我对健康和教育领域的潜力尤为兴奋，相信这些领域将深刻改变整个地区的面貌。（01:20:05）在Latitud，我们除了金融科技外，还重点投资B2B中小企业平台，助力企业规模化运营和提升效率，因为这类需求巨大且存在巨大发展机遇。我相信这些投资将对该地区产生深远影响。所以以上就是我的建议。建议虽略显宽泛，但除此之外，我不会再列举15家我们在Latitud喜欢的公司了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, we can point people to your portfolio page on your website.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们可以引导人们访问你们网站上的投资组合页面。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: I would love to highlight our portfolio companies. Maybe I'll just send you a list or something. I don't know.
turns.zh: 我很想重点介绍我们的投资组合公司。或许我会把一份名单发给你们之类的。我也不确定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect. We will figure out a way to share that. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Gina, are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，我会想办法分享这些信息。说到这，我们已经进入了激动人心的闪电问答环节。吉娜，你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: I'm ready, Lenny.
turns.zh: 我准备好了，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你们向别人推荐得最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: The one book I recommend because I truly, it really changed the way I think about things. It taught me a lot about a discipline I had never really thought much about, but also because I think it makes me sound smart and it's a really short book, so it's easy to get through is The Design Of Everyday Things. For me, that was the first time that I realized that design wasn't just this sort of cool thing that some people were into and they had to get and it made things beautiful. It was about understanding how everything is designed and how to think about design and usability. (01:21:28): So for someone like me who didn't have any experience in product before, I think it could be transformative. And then the second book, it has nothing to do with what we do. I recommend Viktor Frankl's Man's Search For Meaning because at heart I'm a philosopher and I tend to think a lot about life, the meaning of life and what differentiates one life from the next and how to live a good one. And no matter what profession we choose that continues to be important. So those are my recommendations.
turns.zh: 有一本书我推荐得最多，因为它真的改变了我的思维方式。它让我对一个我从未深入思考过的学科有了很多了解，同时也因为我觉得它让我听起来很聪明，而且这本书很短，很容易读完，那就是《设计心理学》。对我来说，这是我第一次意识到设计不只是某些人感兴趣的酷炫事物，它能让事物变得美观。它关乎理解一切事物是如何被设计的，以及如何思考设计和可用性。（01:21:28）所以对于像我这样之前没有产品经验的人来说，它可以带来变革。然后第二本书，与我们所从事的行业无关。我推荐维克多·弗兰克尔的《活出生命的意义》，因为我本质上是个哲学家，我经常思考生命、生命的意义，以及不同生命的区别，以及如何过上美好的生活。无论我们选择何种职业，这一点始终很重要。所以这些就是我的推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite recent movie or TV show that you really enjoy?
turns.zh: 你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: So first of all, I love Succession, but I don't think we have to go into that. One that was recommended to me by a friend who I very much admire was Mike Krieger, co-founder of Instagram is How to with John Wilson. It's a really weird TV show that I would've never found if it wasn't for him. But the premise is basically this guy, I think he's a filmmaker and he's awkward and it's cool that he's awkward. It's just his style and he decides to make a TV show about creating to help people who are really worried or scared of doing something and helping them prepare for that moment in their lives. (01:22:42): So for example, someone is really scared of telling their friends that they lied about how many college degrees they had or whatever that they said they had a master's degree, but they didn't. And it's now been five years and it's not the debate club, but I forget what it is, but something that requires some sort of intellect and he doesn't want to confront the group. And so he recreates everything that could possibly happen that day in order to make this easier. Or another one about having kids. Someone's really scared about making the decision about whether or not they want to have kids. So it's kind of a documentary, but it's not. It's awkward. It's weird, but it's so good. And then I would say White Lotus, just like so good.
turns.zh: 首先，我喜欢《继承之战》，但我觉得我们没必要深入探讨。一个朋友推荐给我的，我非常敬佩的人——Instagram的联合创始人迈克·克里格的节目《How to with John Wilson》。这是一部非常奇特的电视节目，如果不是他，我永远不会发现它。但这个节目的基本设定是，这个家伙，我觉得他是个电影制作人，他很尴尬，但这种尴尬很酷。这就是他的风格，他决定做一个关于创造的电视节目，帮助那些真正担心或害怕做某件事的人，为他们人生的那一刻做好准备。（01:22:42）比如，有人真的害怕告诉朋友自己在大学里撒谎说自己有硕士学位，但实际上并没有。现在已经五年了，这不是辩论俱乐部之类的，但我忘了具体是什么了，但需要某种智力的东西，而他不想面对这个群体。所以他重现了那天可能发生的一切，让这件事变得更容易。或者另一个关于生孩子的。有人真的很害怕是否要生孩子。所以这算是一部纪录片，但又不完全是。很尴尬，很奇特，但真的很棒。然后我要说《白莲花度假村》，也很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I do that song to my new child often because it's so funny.
turns.zh: 我经常把那首歌唱给我的新孩子听，因为它太有趣了。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: My husband and I do it at home.
turns.zh: 我丈夫和我在家也会这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Lot is a recurring,
turns.zh: “Lot”是反复出现的，

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: Yeah,
turns.zh: 是的，

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I'm not going to do it, but it's a recurring favorite on this podcast. So we had a short drinking game where every time someone said, White Lotus, we drink. So I'm going to have some tea here real quick.
turns.zh: 是的。我不会做，但这是这个播客上反复出现的最爱。所以我们玩了一个简短的喝酒游戏，每次有人说《白莲花度假村》，我们就喝一杯。所以我现在要快速喝点茶。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: Okay. I'm sorry to be predictable, but like I said-
turns.zh: 好的。很抱歉我有点老生常谈，但就像我说的那样——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No its great.
turns.zh: 不，这很棒。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: We humans are a lot more similar than we'd like to think. What's amazing Lenny is just my realization more and more of how much this is true because I like to think of myself as unique much like everybody else. And then I started seeing that all of these really creative decisions I made are what all of the other millennial white girls did. It's just fascinating. Oh, I like whatever, mid-century modern furniture. Oh, you know what? Actually, I'll tell you what movie is my favorite one? Bo Burnham's Inside. I love-
turns.zh: 人类之间的相似性远超我们想象。莱尼，真正让我意识到这一点的是，我曾自以为独一无二，但后来发现自己做的许多创造性决策，原来其他千禧一代白人女性也都做过。这真是太神奇了。哦，我喜欢中世纪现代风格家具。哦，你知道吗？说到电影，我最喜欢的还是博·伯纳姆的《内在美》。我超爱这部片子——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God,
turns.zh: 天啊,

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: I don't know if that's a movie, but I'm in love with Bo Burnham. My husband knows about this. I know all of the songs and what is it? White Girl's, Instagram? White Woman's Instagram. Such a good song. That's what I'm talking about.
turns.zh: 我不确定这是不是部电影，但我超迷博·伯纳姆。我丈夫都知道这些。我熟悉他所有的歌曲，还有什么《白人女孩的Instagram》？还是《白人女性的Instagram》？那首歌太棒了。这就是我想说的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also, I've been re-listening to How is the best case scenario, Joe Biden,
turns.zh: 另外，我最近又重温了乔·拜登的《最佳情况假设》。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: They're going to make me vote for Joe Biden. I was singing this to my parents. They didn't get it.
turns.zh: 他们非要让我投票给乔·拜登。我还给父母唱过这首歌，他们完全听不懂。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. We'll link to that video, that movie. It's even after COVID, it's incredible. Anyway, I was actually going to say that first show you mentioned, I think it's called The Rehearsal, maybe there's a different title.
turns.zh: 太神奇了。我们会附上那部电影的链接，甚至在新冠疫情之后，它依然令人惊叹。总之，我本来想提到你提到的第一部剧集，好像叫《排练》？可能还有个不同的名字。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: Oh my gosh, you're right. So he has two shows and one of them is called How To and the other one is called The Rehearsal. And you're right, I am recommending the rehearsal. I have also seen How To, which are shorter episodes where he films in New York and he just goes like How to find a parking spot. And then it takes him on this down a rabbit hole of how cars are made or parking in the city. But it's also very good. But I prefer The Rehearsal.
turns.zh: 天啊，你说得对。他有两部作品，一部叫《How To》，另一部叫《排练》。你说得对，我推荐《排练》。我也看过《How To》，每集较短，拍摄于纽约，比如如何找停车位，然后顺便深入探讨汽车制造或城市停车难题。不过《排练》更棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And Nathan Fielder's the guy behind all this who's incredibly hilarious. He has a new show, actually I think it's on HBO with John Wilson or something that he's producing or it's this other guy. He's going around talking about stuff in New York and I think he's a producer.
turns.zh: 内森·菲尔德是幕后主创，超级搞笑。他还有新剧，好像在HBO和约翰·威尔逊合作制作，或者是和别人合作的。他在纽约四处探访各种事物，我觉得他是个制片人。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: That's the one I'm talking about. That's How To with John Wilson.
turns.zh: 就是我说的那个节目《How To with John Wilson》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, there we go. So I think he's behind that. Okay, look at us. We're figuring things out.
turns.zh: 哦，找到了！所以我觉得是他主导的。好吧，看看我们现在的情况。我们正在理清思路。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: We are figuring things out. So I think he has maybe a new season.
turns.zh: 我们正在理清思路。所以我觉得他可能有新一季了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Think season two. I haven't started that one yet. Anyway, here we go. We're going to keep going. What is a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates that you're interviewing?
turns.zh: 应该是第二季吧。我还没开始看呢。总之，继续吧。你最喜欢问面试候选人的哪个问题？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: Why do you want to work here is what I really like to ask because it tells me a lot. Of course, everyone wants a job. People could just be like, because I want a job and it seems like you guys pay well and whatever. I think this is a good next step in my career, but I want to know if this person knows what it is that we do, if they did a minimum level of research and if they connect with our mission because we're going to talk about mission a lot and I don't want them to gloss over it and to make decisions that are short-term thinking that go against our mission because of the reasons I mentioned with Duolingo. So I think that's one, it's not very unique, but I think gives you a lot of information. And then I would say, what are you world-class at and how do you know that you're at that? (01:26:41): And the second part is almost more important. What are you world class at? It's okay if someone says, look, I'm working on becoming world class at whatever, and this is why I think I'm great at it or whatever. But the second part is important because it tells me if people actually care about metrics, and I don't care what the metrics are, but just how do you know this to be true? It has to be more than like, "Oh, because my boss loves me," or "Because my mom told me," "because I gave a talk," or whatnot or whatever I want to hear, "I'm proud of having accomplished this." And maybe if you have some numbers to show, that's also really important.
turns.zh: 你们为什么想来这里工作？这正是我最想问的，因为这能透露很多信息。当然，每个人都想找份工作，他们可能会说"因为我需要一份工作"，或者"你们公司薪资不错之类的"。但我认为这只是职业生涯的下一步。我想知道应聘者是否了解我们的业务，是否做过最基本的调研，以及他们是否认同我们的使命——毕竟我们会经常谈论使命，不希望他们敷衍了事，或者因为某些短视的原因做出违背使命的决策，就像我之前在Duolingo遇到的情况。所以我认为这第一个问题虽然不算独特，但能提供大量信息。接下来我想问，你在哪个领域堪称世界级专家？（01:26:41）第二个问题更重要。什么叫世界级？有人可能会说"我正在努力成为某个领域的世界级专家"，或者"因为我老板认可我"，或者"因为我妈妈这么说"，或者"因为我做过演讲"之类的。但更关键的是：你如何确定自己的能力？不能只是"因为老板喜欢我"，或者"因为妈妈这么说"，或者"因为我参加过演讲"之类的。我希望听到更真诚的回答，比如"我对数据有深刻理解"，或者"我对市场有敏锐洞察"之类的。如果能拿出数据支持，那就更好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite product that you recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: I have not been trying any products, I would say. So nothing to recommend. I would say though that I am very curious to try these gut health tests that are out there now or microbiome ones. I'm really interested in how little we know about our body and how tech can actually help democratize this information. And going on a tiny rant. I'm also feeling very resentful of doctors right now because we've always lived in a world in which doctors are sort of like these authorities and we must just believe whatever it is that they tell us, and we rely on them for information that is crucial to our survival. (01:27:58): But we're now in a world where we can Google things and that's even more scary because you have to know how to filter that information really well and you don't find explanations to things. But doctors don't like you Googling because they say it's scary, but also because they don't like being questioned. I think we're finally coming to a place where a lot of these devices that can give you great information about your body so that you understand your nutrition and very core things about ourselves that we don't today are becoming accessible to a lot of people just to the population. It's still expensive but we're getting there, and I think that will be magical. So I will call out the company Levels by my friend Sam Corcos because I think that what they're doing is awesome.
turns.zh: 我最近没尝试什么新产品，所以没什么推荐。不过我很想试试现在市面上的肠道健康检测产品，或者微生物组检测产品。我对我们对自身身体知之甚少感到好奇，也很想看看科技如何能让这些信息更普及。说点题外话，我现在对医生很不满。我们一直生活在医生是权威的世界里，必须无条件相信他们的说法，还要依赖他们提供关乎生命的信息。但现在我们能用谷歌搜索信息，这更可怕了，因为要学会筛选信息，还找不到权威解释。但医生不喜欢你用谷歌，他们说这危险，又不喜欢被质疑。我觉得我们终于迎来了一个时代，许多能提供身体信息的设备，让人们了解营养状况和自身核心健康的知识正在普及，虽然价格还高，但方向是正确的，我觉得这会带来革命性变化。这里要表扬一下我朋友Sam Corcos的公司Levels，他们做的事太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next question. What is a favorite life motto that you like to think about? Come back to share with other people.
turns.zh: 下一个问题。有没有喜欢的座右铭？回来和大家分享一下。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: One is "This too shall pass." And I will tell you this one right now is particularly meaningful to me right now because I'm going through a really tough moment because I have long COVID and lost my taste and smell, and it might be long-term. So, but I think it applies to the A/B thing that I was talking about when everything in life is moments except for a couple of diagnoses. And so, "This too shall pass," is something I say to myself a lot. The second one is also not particularly motivational, but I really believe in it, which is, "Fake it till you make it." That's something I've held onto for a long time. And even today, I don't mean lie. I don't mean pretend to be something that you're not, but it's almost like a way to overcome imposter syndrome and by opening rooms for yourself to be who you want to become so that you enable opportunities to become that. (01:29:39): And I'm not saying lying, but early in my career, I did fake it until I make it from the point of view of not saying no to things. When companies were saying to me being like, "Hey, can you help us grow without a budget like Tumblr," right? I was 25, 26. I was like, "Yeah, and then go figure it out." And when Duolingo turned to me and said, "Hey, can you be head of growth?" And I didn't know what growth was and I had to Google and find Andrew Chen's blog, I read it and I found out and I just said, "Yes," and then kept going with that. So fake it till you make it as kind of that for me. (01:30:07): But even today I have a lot of imposter syndrome, which I actually think is not imposter syndrome, is just acknowledging that I don't know a lot. My team says I have too much self-deprecating humor that actually puts the company down. It puts me down. So fake it till you make it to me means knowing how to stand in front of your team or a reporter or Lenny in a podcast and almost like being that person that you would like to be or being your best self. You could call it whatever you want, but I think it can really help you get out of the little hole that you would put yourself into and limit opportunities for yourself.
turns.zh:
其中一个是“这也会过去的”。我现在要告诉你们，这句话对我来说意义非凡，因为我正经历一段非常艰难的时期——我患了长期新冠，失去了味觉和嗅觉，而且这种情况可能长期存在。不过，我认为这适用于我之前提到的A/B测试问题。生活中除了某些特定的时刻，其余都是转瞬即逝的。所以，“这也会过去的”，我经常这样告诉自己。

第二个说法也不算特别励志，但我深信其中的道理，那就是“先假装成功，直到真的成功”。这句话我坚持了很久。即使在今天，我不是说要撒谎，也不是要伪装成不是自己的样子，而是要克服冒名顶替综合症，为自己创造机会，成为理想中的自己。

（01:29:39）：我不是说要撒谎，但在职业生涯早期，我确实用过“先假装成功，直到真的成功”这种策略，尤其是在面对机会时。当时公司对我说，你能帮我们像Tumblr那样在没有预算的情况下促进增长吗？那时我25、26岁，我回答：“可以，然后你自己想办法解决。” 而当Duolingo找我时，他们问：“你能担任增长部门主管吗？”我当时对增长一无所知，不得不谷歌搜索Andrew Chen的博客，读完后才明白，然后就答应了。所以对我来说，“先假装成功，直到真的成功”就是这样一种心态。

（01:30:07）：但即使现在，我仍深受冒名顶替综合症的困扰。我觉得这其实不是冒名顶替症，而是承认自己有很多东西不了解。我的团队说我自嘲太多，把公司贬低了，也贬低了自己。对我来说，“先假装成功，直到真的成功”意味着要知道如何站在团队面前、面对记者或像Lenny这样的人时，表现出理想中的自己，或者展现出最好的自己。你可以随意称呼它，但我认为它真的能帮助你走出自设的困境，抓住机会。
